newsitem.title: USA: U.S. welcomes EU tougher line on Iran.
newsitem.headline: U.S. welcomes EU tougher line on Iran.

text.p: The United States welcomed a European Union decision on Tuesday to suspend ministerial ties with Iran and said the former EU policy of "critical dialogue" with Tehran was now dead.

The State Department said the EU shared the U.S. view "that Iran must respect the norms of international law, refrain from acts of terrorism and live up to international commitments on human rights and on proliferation issues."
Spokesman Nicholas Burns was responding to a decision taken in Luxembourg by EU foreign ministers following a German court finding that Iran's rulers had ordered political assassinations in Germany.
The ministers decided to continue an arms embargo on Iran, refuse visas to Iranians with intelligence or security roles and move to bar all Iranian intelligence agents from Europe.
But they agreed that ambassadors called home from Tehran three weeks ago could now return if their governments wished.
"In an ideal, perfect world, we would have preferred an agreement on complete isolation of Iran," Burns said.

"That hasn't happened, the EU ambassadors are going back," he said. "But when they go back, they will go back with this very tough message that it's not going to be business as usual any longer between the European Union members states and the government of Iran."
"The critical dialogue is dead and we very much appreciate the fact that the European Union member countries have acted decisively today to send a clear message to Iran," Burns said.
"It's a result that has resolve and backbone behind it, and we're very pleased with where they ended up in Luxembourg ... This is an appreciable change in Europe's policy towards Iran," he said.

The "critical dialogue" policy was agreed by the EU in 1992 as a way of maintaining ties and trading relationships while seeking to change Iran's behaviour. It was derided by the United States as a total failure.

Former U.S. Under Secretary of State Peter Tarnoff toured EU capitals last week trying to get the Europeans to adopt as strong a line as possible on Iran, and Burns suggested the mission had been a partial success.

"Obviously we would have preferred if the Europeans had included the threat of additional economic sanctions in case Iranian behaviour does not improve ... But I think we have to be realistic," he said.
EU and other countries have refused to join the United States in trade sanctions on Iran. But Burns said Washington looked forward to working with the Europeans to develop a "realistic" policy.
